cards.explanation: The answer is standing in awe. Habakkuk says, "…I have heard the report of You; I stand in awe, O LORD, of Your deeds." (Habakkuk 3:2) He heard the report, and he stands in awe of what the LORD has done. I think he's standing there with his mouth open, friends.

The answer is to revive them and make them known. Habakkuk asks, "Revive them in these years; make them known in these years." (Habakkuk 3:2) He's heard what the LORD has done, and he wants those deeds alive in his own time. Notice he says "these years" twice. I think he means it, like a man tapping the table.

The answer is mercy. "In Your wrath, remember mercy!" (Habakkuk 3:2) That's a short prayer with a big ask, friends. Habakkuk sets wrath and mercy side by side and asks for mercy to be remembered. I think a prayer this honest is hard to pray, and he prays it anyway.

The answer is True. Habakkuk says, "…His glory covered the heavens, and His praise filled the earth." (Habakkuk 3:3) The heavens are covered and the earth is filled. There's not a corner left over. That's a whole lot of glory, friends.

The answer is True. Habakkuk says, "rays flashed from His hand, where His power is hidden." (Habakkuk 3:4) The rays flash from His hand, and that's where the power is hidden. If that's what the hand looks like, I'd say take a seat and listen, friends. I think this is a prophet who knows he's looking at something big.

The answer is plague and fever. Habakkuk says, "Plague went before Him, and fever followed in His steps." (Habakkuk 3:5) One out in front and one right behind. That's a picture of a very serious arrival. It's a heavy line, so I'll let the text speak for itself.

The answer is False. God stands, measures the earth and startles the nations, and "the ancient mountains crumbled; the perpetual hills collapsed." (Habakkuk 3:6) Mountains are the thing we call solid. Meanwhile I can't even get my dough to hold its shape.

The answer is that they are everlasting. Habakkuk says, "His ways are everlasting." (Habakkuk 3:6) Look at what comes right before it: ancient mountains crumbling and perpetual hills collapsing. Those are the things we call permanent, and they go down. His ways don't.
The answer is tents in distress. Habakkuk says, "I saw the tents of Cushan in distress…" (Habakkuk 3:7) Cushan is the first of two names in that verse. Distress is the picture he gives.

The answer is that the deep roars and lifts its hands. Habakkuk says, "The deep roared with its voice and lifted its hands on high." (Habakkuk 3:10) He pictures the deep like a person, loud and with its hands up. When the mountains quake and the water sweeps by, even the deep joins in. That's some crowd, friends.

The answer is True. Habakkuk says, "You marched across the earth with fury; You threshed the nations in wrath." (Habakkuk 3:12) This is a heavy part of the prayer, and I won't dress it up. Habakkuk says it straight, and so does the text.

The answer is save. Habakkuk says, "You went forth for the salvation of Your people, to save Your anointed." (Habakkuk 3:13) The verse before has the fury and the wrath. This verse names what He went forth for: salvation. Both are in the same prayer, and the text lets them stand together.

The answer is the wicked one's own spear. Habakkuk says, "With his own spear You pierced his head…" (Habakkuk 3:14) It was his own spear, and the verse says it plainly. This is a heavy line, so I'll leave it at what the text says. The same verse says his warriors stormed out to scatter us.

The answer is False. Habakkuk says the warriors came out "…gloating as though ready to secretly devour the weak." (Habakkuk 3:14) The word is weak, not strong. The whole thing is a heavy picture, and one word changes it.

The answer is that they churn. Habakkuk says, "You trampled the sea with Your horses, churning the great waters." (Habakkuk 3:15) The waters churn. We're back at the sea from earlier in the prayer, and it's still stirred up. That's a whole lot of water getting tossed around.

The answer is that he trembles. Habakkuk says, "I heard and trembled within; my lips quivered at the sound." (Habakkuk 3:16) He trembles within, and his lips quiver at the sound. A prayer that big goes right through a man. I think anyone would shake after hearing all that.

The answer is invaders. Habakkuk says, "Yet I must wait patiently for the day of distress to come upon the people who invade us." (Habakkuk 3:16) He's shaking inside, and he still says he must wait patiently. That's a hard kind of waiting. I think waiting and shaking at the same time is its own skill.

The answer is False. Habakkuk's list goes past the crops. He says, "…the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls…" (Habakkuk 3:17) So the sheep and cattle are in the list too, right along with the crops.

The answer is to rejoice in the LORD. Habakkuk says, "…yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!" (Habakkuk 3:18) The list before it is full of things that aren't happening, and he still says yet. That one little word carries the whole verse. This is the happiest part of the prayer.

The answer is True. Habakkuk says, "GOD the Lord is my strength…" (Habakkuk 3:19) He says it after that whole list of crops and animals. The Lord is his strength, plain and simple. I think that's a sturdy place to stand.

The answer is deer. Habakkuk says, "He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights!" (Habakkuk 3:19) A deer and the heights go together nicely. I think it's a picture of a man with steady feet in high places. Not bad for someone who was trembling a few verses ago.
